## Introduction

In the GitHub Introduction tutorial, you compared a raw Codespace with your own and reproduced each of `connect-repo`'s steps by hand, against a throwaway repo. `connect-repo` is a convenience script that lives in `codespace-starter` --- a repo you do not control, and a script that might change or disappear. By the end of this tutorial, that will not matter: you will have run the entire repo lifecycle --- create, connect, work, push, clone onto a fresh machine, pull, and dispose --- with your own hands.

So, unlike every other tutorial: **do not run `connect-repo` today.**

Some material is from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. The most useful reference for Git/GitHub is [*Happy Git and GitHub for the useR*](https://happygitwithr.com/).

## A repo by hand

Everything in this section happens in your current Codespace. You will make the repo this tutorial is named for --- `github-advanced` --- using only `gh` and `git`.

### Exercise 1

Open a new bash Terminal and run `cd /workspaces`. (New terminals may open inside the repo from an earlier tutorial. That auto-jump is a `connect-repo` convenience. From now on, we `cd` ourselves.) Then run `gh auth status`.

If it reports that you are **not** logged in, run these four commands, the sign-in steps from the GitHub Introduction tutorial, and then run `gh auth status` again:

```bash
unset GITHUB_TOKEN GH_TOKEN
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false
git config --global credential.helper store
printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\n' "$(gh auth token)" > ~/.git-credentials
```

For the login, `gh` first asks `Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? (Y/n)` --- press `Enter`. It then shows a one-time code and says `Press Enter to open https://github.com/login/device in your browser...`. Press `Enter`, paste the code into the GitHub tab that opens, and come back to the Terminal.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: a-repo-by-hand-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Open a new bash Terminal and run cd /workspaces. (New terminals may open inside the repo from an earlier tutorial. That auto-jump is a connect-repo convenience. From now on, we cd ourselves.) Then run gh auth status. If it reports that you are not logged in, run these four commands, the sign-in steps from the GitHub Introduction tutorial, and then run gh auth status again: unset GITHUB_TOKEN GH_TOKEN, then gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false, then git config --global credential.helper store, then printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\\n' \"$(gh auth token)\" > ~/.git-credentials. For the login, gh first asks Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? (Y/n), press Enter. It then shows a one-time code and says Press Enter to open https://github.com/login/device in your browser... Press Enter, paste the code into the GitHub tab that opens, and come back to the Terminal. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
workspaces $ gh auth status
github.com
  ✓ Logged in to github.com account your-username (/home/rstudio/.config/gh/hosts.yml)
  - Active account: true
  - Git operations protocol: https
  - Token: gho_************************************
  - Token scopes: 'gist', 'read:org', 'repo', 'workflow'
```

If you were not signed in, the first `gh auth status` said so instead, and the second one looks like the above:

```{.output}
workspaces $ gh auth status
You are not logged into any GitHub hosts. To log in, run: gh auth login
```

###

You were probably already signed in --- `connect-repo` did that once, in some earlier session, and `gh` keeps the login in the file named in parentheses, `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`. That file lives in *this* Codespace only: a fresh Codespace is logged out. Every `git` and `gh` command you run --- and every AI agent that pushes code on your behalf --- uses exactly these credentials.

### Exercise 2

Create this tutorial's repo by hand. From `/workspaces`, run:

```bash
gh repo create github-advanced --public --clone
```

If GitHub says a repository by that name already exists (from an earlier attempt, say), run `gh repo clone github-advanced` instead.

Then run `ls`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: a-repo-by-hand-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Create this tutorial's repo by hand. From /workspaces, run gh repo create github-advanced --public --clone. If GitHub says a repository by that name already exists (from an earlier attempt, say), run gh repo clone github-advanced instead. Then run ls. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
workspaces $ gh repo create github-advanced --public --clone
✓ Created repository your-username/github-advanced on github.com
  https://github.com/your-username/github-advanced
workspaces $ ls
codespace-starter  github-advanced
workspaces $
```

Your `ls` may also show repos from earlier tutorials. Nothing was downloaded: a brand-new repo has no commits yet, so `--clone` just makes the folder and wires it to GitHub.

###

Why `--public`? GitHub repos are either **public** or **private**. A public repo is visible to anyone on the internet --- not just people you share the link with. A private repo is visible only to you and collaborators you explicitly invite. We use public repos in this course, which is also what lets GitHub Pages host your work for free. For work that should stay private, `gh repo create <name> --private --clone` is the only change you need.

###

`AGENTS.md` is just a file that `connect-repo` copies into every new repo. It tells AI assistants how to work with you. With it in place, you have done by hand everything the script does that matters: the sign-in, the credential store that makes it last, the repo creation, the clone, and the window switch. The script's remaining conveniences --- opening new terminals in your repo, dropping the terminal that ran it into the repo, silencing the READY banner --- are cosmetic.

### Exercise 6

Before committing, see what Git sees. Run `git status`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: a-repo-by-hand-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Before committing, see what Git sees. Run git status. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
github-advanced $ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        .gitignore
        AGENTS.md
        analysis.html
        analysis.qmd

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```

###

Note what is *not* listed: `analysis_files`, because your `.gitignore` is already working. `git status` shows exactly the same information as the Source Control pane --- untracked files there wear a "U" --- just in text form. Knowing the text version means you know what the buttons actually do, and it is how you check up on an AI agent's work in your repo.

### Exercise 7

Make the first push. Run these three commands, one at a time:

```bash
git add -A
git commit -m "First analysis"
git push -u origin main
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: a-repo-by-hand-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Make the first push. Run these three commands, one at a time: git add -A, then git commit -m \"First analysis\", then git push -u origin main. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
github-advanced $ git add -A
github-advanced $ git commit -m "First analysis"
[main (root-commit) 1a2b3c4] First analysis
 4 files changed, 152 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 AGENTS.md
 create mode 100644 analysis.html
 create mode 100644 analysis.qmd
github-advanced $ git push -u origin main
Enumerating objects: 6, done.
Writing objects: 100% (6/6), 24.31 KiB | 8.10 MiB/s, done.
To https://github.com/your-username/github-advanced.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
github-advanced $
```

###

The new piece is `-u` (for `--set-upstream`). A brand-new repo's `main` branch does not yet know which remote branch it corresponds to, so the very first push must say so: `-u origin main` means "push to `origin`, and remember this pairing." After that, plain `git push` works forever. (Some setups configure Git to do this automatically, in which case plain `git push` succeeds even the first time. `-u` is still the portable habit that works everywhere.) `root-commit` in the commit output marks the first commit in the repo's entire history.

## A second desk

A machine you have never touched --- your own laptop, a colleague's Codespace, a fresh cloud server --- has no `connect-repo` and no credentials. Codespaces make fresh machines cheap, so this section uses one.

### Exercise 1

In a **new browser tab**, go to [github.com/codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces). Click the green **New codespace** button, choose the repository `PPBDS/codespace-starter`, leave the branch as `main`, and click **Create codespace**. When the new window asks whether you trust the authors of the files in this folder, click **Trust Folder & Continue**.

Keep the tutorial tab open! You now have two Codespaces: the one running this tutorial, and a fresh machine. The boot takes a minute or so. When it finishes, the Panel holds one bash terminal showing the READY banner, which tells you to run `connect-repo`. Ignore that today. (The small warning icon on that terminal's tab is harmless.)

Copy and paste the new Codespace's URL (from its browser tab, ending in `.github.dev`).

```{r}
#| label: a-second-desk-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Copy and paste the new Codespace's URL (from its browser tab, ending in .github.dev).",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
https://zany-computing-machine-vpvrv9p59jxpc66v6.github.dev/
```

###

While you waited, GitHub built a computer from the instructions in `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` inside `codespace-starter`. The key line there names a pre-built image, `ghcr.io/ppbds/devcontainer:1.3.1`, with R, the tidyverse, Quarto, and the rest already inside. The file then adds the editor extensions and settings on top. Nothing is installed at startup --- the image is downloaded and switched on --- which is why every Codespace boots quickly and arrives identical to every other.

### Exercise 2

In the **new** Codespace, use the bash Terminal that is already open --- it has the short prompt, `codespace-starter $` --- and run the sign-in ritual by hand. This machine has never met you, so this time the sign-in is needed. Run these commands, one at a time:

```bash
unset GITHUB_TOKEN GH_TOKEN
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false
git config --global credential.helper store
printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\n' "$(gh auth token)" > ~/.git-credentials
gh auth status
```

For the login, follow the prompts in order: press `Enter` at `Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? (Y/n)`, copy the one-time code, press `Enter` at `Press Enter to open https://github.com/login/device in your browser...`, paste the code into the GitHub tab that opens, and return. CP/CR the final `gh auth status` output.

```{r}
#| label: a-second-desk-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the new Codespace, use the bash Terminal that is already open, it has the short prompt, codespace-starter $, and run the sign-in ritual by hand. This machine has never met you, so this time the sign-in is needed. Run these commands, one at a time: unset GITHUB_TOKEN GH_TOKEN, then gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false, then git config --global credential.helper store, then printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\\n' \"$(gh auth token)\" > ~/.git-credentials, then gh auth status. For the login, follow the prompts in order: press Enter at Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? (Y/n), copy the one-time code, press Enter at Press Enter to open https://github.com/login/device in your browser..., paste the code into the GitHub tab that opens, and return. CP/CR the final gh auth status output.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

The login itself ends like this:

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false
? Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? Yes

! First copy your one-time code: 5076-D3B6
Press Enter to open https://github.com/login/device in your browser... 
✓ Authentication complete.
- gh config set -h github.com git_protocol https
✓ Configured git protocol
! Authentication credentials saved in plain text
✓ Logged in as your-username
codespace-starter $
```

And the final `gh auth status`:

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ gh auth status
github.com
  ✓ Logged in to github.com account your-username (/home/rstudio/.config/gh/hosts.yml)
  - Active account: true
  - Git operations protocol: https
  - Token: gho_************************************
  - Token scopes: 'gist', 'read:org', 'repo', 'workflow'
```

###

Why the `unset`? A Codespace starts with a built-in token that acts as the *Codespace*, not as *you* --- it can read `codespace-starter` and nothing more. Clearing it forces `gh` to use your real login instead. This whole ritual happens once per machine. On your own laptop, the equivalent is installing `gh` and running `gh auth login` --- same command, no `unset` needed.

Why step 3? `gh auth login` hands your token to Git, but only to Git's short-term memory: the Codespace comes configured with a credential *cache* that forgets after an hour. Skip step 3 and `git push` works for an hour, then stops at `Username for 'https://github.com':`. `git config --global credential.helper store` tells Git to also keep the token in a file, `~/.git-credentials`. The `printf` line writes your token into that file now: `gh auth token` prints it, and `>` puts it there. From then on every push from this Codespace goes out as you. `connect-repo` goes one step further and makes that file the *only* place Git looks. That is what lets the Source Control pane's Sync button --- whose copy of Git still carries the Codespace's built-in token --- push as you too. If a push ever does stop at the `Username` prompt, press `Ctrl + C` and run the login command again.

### Exercise 5

Return to your **original** Codespace --- the tab running this tutorial. Its copy of `github-advanced` does not know about the new commit yet. In a bash Terminal there (make sure `pwd` says `/workspaces/github-advanced`), run `git status`. CP/CR.


###

```{.output}
github-advanced $ git status
On branch main
Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 1 commit, and can be fast-forwarded.
  (use "git pull" to update your local branch)

nothing to commit, working tree clean
github-advanced $
```

If yours says `Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'` instead, that is normal too. The next exercise explains why.

###

`git status` never contacts GitHub. It compares your branch with the last snapshot of `origin` this Codespace fetched. VS Code fetches in the background every few minutes, which is why it could report that you were behind. Left to itself, it would have said "up to date" and been wrong.

### Exercise 6

Now bring the commit in. Run `git pull`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: a-second-desk-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the same bash Terminal of your original Codespace, run git pull. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
github-advanced $ git pull
Updating 1a2b3c4..5d6e7f8
Fast-forward
 analysis.qmd | 2 ++
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
github-advanced $
```

If your `git status` said you were up to date, `git pull` also prints a few `remote:` lines as it downloads the commit.

###

`git pull` asks GitHub, fetches anything new, and merges it into your branch. **Push sends, pull receives.** The Source Control pane's "Sync" button does both at once. Whenever more than one desk touches a repo --- a second machine, a collaborator, an AI agent working in the cloud --- pull before you work.

## Disposable desks

Two Codespaces now hold copies of `github-advanced`, and GitHub holds a third. The GitHub copy is the one that matters.

###

```{.output}
github-advanced $ git log --oneline
5d6e7f8 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Add a line from the second machine
1a2b3c4 First analysis
github-advanced $
```

###

The machine that wrote the second commit no longer exists, and the commit survives. It lives on GitHub and on every machine that has pulled it. This is why we commit and push so often: not to save work *to* a Codespace, but to save it *through* the Codespace to GitHub.

## Summary

You ran the entire repo lifecycle without `connect-repo`: signed in with `gh auth login` and made it stick with `git config --global credential.helper store` and a token written to `~/.git-credentials`, created a repo with `gh repo create --public --clone`, inspected its wiring with `git remote -v`, pushed a first commit with `git push -u origin main`, cloned onto a brand-new machine with `gh repo clone`, pushed from there with plain `git push`, brought the change home with `git pull`, and deleted a Codespace without losing a byte.

These are the commands you now own:

```bash
gh auth login                                # once per machine
git config --global credential.helper store  # once per machine, right after the login
printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\n' "$(gh auth token)" > ~/.git-credentials   # once per machine, right after that
gh repo create <name> --public --clone
gh repo clone <name>
git status
git add -A
git commit -m "message"
git push -u origin main   # first push of a new branch
git push                  # every push after that
git pull
git remote -v
git log --oneline
```

`connect-repo` is a convenience, not a dependency.

The three "once per machine" lines are the only part of this that is still a chore, and the next tutorial, "Dotfiles," retires them: a brand new Codespace will arrive already signed in as you.
